$comment: Rules for scripts/history-scan.mjs — the pre-open history scrub audit of
insimul-native (docs/explanation/OPEN_SOURCE_STRATEGY.md, 'Pre-open
checklist' → History scrub; tasklist 242-pre-open-native US-1).
The pattern set is INHERITED from insimul/core@b37837b's
scripts/history-scan.rules.json — 241 is the probe, 242 reuses its method —
plus the rules below marked 'native-specific', which cover the classes core
does not have: a vendored C engine, a vendored JS engine, build outputs that
are binary, and a committed benchmark world.
Two rule kinds, and the difference matters:
path    — matched against the object's path in history. Catches a class of
file that must never exist in an open repo at all (.env, key
material, the closed data/insimul/** pack tree, a shipped binary).
content — matched against the blob's decoded text. Catches a credential
pasted into a file whose NAME is innocent, which is how secrets
actually reach a repository.
A third detector is STRUCTURAL and lives in code, not here: the pack-shape
detector in scripts/check-pack-provenance.mjs (vendored from core byte for
byte). It is deliberately not a pattern list, because a deny-list of the
closed tables' real values would have to contain the real values in the open
repository — the leak it is meant to prevent, wearing a guard's clothes.
Each rule declares a `classification`:
scrub  — if this ever matches, the history must be rewritten before the flip.
review — the pattern is suggestive but not conclusive; a human classifies
the finding keep/scrub and records the decision in `allow` below.
An unclassified match is never silently keep: --check exits non-zero on any
finding that is not covered by an `allow` entry.
Patterns are JavaScript regular expressions. A leading `(?i)` — which JS does
not support inline — is translated by the scanner into the `i` flag; anywhere
else in a pattern it is an error rather than a silently-dead group.

rules.description: The closed genre/language world packs and generation heuristics (data/insimul/**, OPEN_SOURCE_STRATEGY.md 'The content boundary'). These are the CLOSED asset; a single historical commit publishes them forever. This repository has never had one — the rule is the guard that says so, and it stays whether or not it fires.

native-specific. A directory of world/pack content. libinsimul is the ENGINE — the thing that runs a world — and a world committed into it is either a fixture (fine, and classified as one) or a piece of the closed authoring content that must never be here. `bench/world/` is the committed benchmark fixture and is classified in `allow`; anything else that lands under this pattern needs a human before the flip.

A .pl source. The Prolog ENGINE is open and contract-level base predicates ship; the genre bundles, the language corpora (CEFR/SRS data, the ~573 .pl seed files) and the generation heuristics do not. Every .pl in history is therefore classified by hand — see `allow`. In this repository most of them are the vendored engine's own library.

native-specific. A compiled or packaged artifact by extension. Two reasons it is a finding rather than a nuisance: this repository BUILDS wasm modules, preload images, static libraries and dist tarballs, so a committed one is a real possibility; and the scanner cannot read any of them, so a binary blob in history is a hole in the audit that a human has to close by knowing what it is. `.data` is Emscripten's preload image — the one artifact here that can carry a whole Prolog library tree inside it.

native-specific. A build or dependency tree that .gitignore is supposed to keep out (build/, build-wasm/, dist/, node_modules/, rust's target/). Committed build output is how a binary — engine objects, a preload image, a packaged shared library — reaches a history that reads as pure source, and it is invisible to any working-tree check once removed.

A committed .env. Whatever it held was live when it was committed and must be assumed compromised, so this is scrub-AND-rotate, not scrub alone. .env.example / .env.sample / .env.template are excluded by `except`.
Private key material by filename: PEM/PKCS#12/Java keystores and SSH private keys.

Files whose normal contents are credentials — .npmrc (registry auth token), .netrc, cloud CLI credential files. Often committed empty or with only a registry URL, which is why this is review and not scrub.
AWS access key id.
GitHub personal access / OAuth / app token, classic and fine-grained.
Anthropic API key.
OpenAI API key (legacy sk-… and sk-proj-… project keys).
Google / Firebase API key.
Slack bot/user/app token.
Stripe live secret or restricted key.
npm automation/publish token. This repository publishes @insimul/prolog-wasm (scripts/package.sh --target wasm), so a leaked one is a write credential against a package other repositories install.
An inline PEM private key block, in a file of any name.
A three-segment JWT. Frequently an expired example in a doc, which is why it is review — but a session or service token pasted into a test fixture looks identical.
A database/broker URL carrying inline credentials. Placeholders (user:password@localhost) are common in docs; a real host is not.

A secret-shaped assignment: apiKey/secret/password/token = "<12+ non-space chars>". The broadest rule here and the noisiest by design — it is the one that catches a credential from a vendor nobody wrote a pattern for. Placeholder-looking values are filtered by `except`.

$comment: The structural pack detector, applied to every historical blob. Prefixes
match core's `pack-provenance` script: a real pack is named for the product
it belongs to, so renaming one into this set to get past the check is not a
mistake anybody makes by accident.

allow.reason: The vendored Prolog ENGINE's own standard library (39 files: lists, assoc, dcgs, clpz, format, …), not authoring content. It is upstream Trealla's `library/` directory at the pinned commit 07de013677af760a8bca0594ae4b2bef158a3cde, licensed BSD-2-Clause (docs/TREALLA_LICENSE_FINDING.md §4), and the bytes on disk are PROVEN to be upstream's by tests/run_trealla_vendor.sh, which recomputes git's own tree/blob ids for every vendored path offline. So this is not a judgement about 39 files nobody read: it is a judgement about one pinned upstream directory whose identity is already a ctest. A prefix allowance rather than 39 entries — see allowanceFor() in history-scan.mjs for why that is the safer of the two.

The ABI bootstrap — the Prolog that IS libinsimul's C layer (running goals, serialising the binding-set JSON, classifying ISO errors, snapshotting). Every promise include/insimul.h makes is implemented here. It is engine plumbing, the open half of the content boundary by definition: a runtime cannot be shown conformant against an ABI whose implementation it cannot read. No genre bundle, no language corpus, no generation heuristic. Five blobs = five revisions of the same file.

The golden snapshot image the `snapshot_parse` ctest parses with the wrappers' real prolog-fact-parser.ts. Six clauses of throwaway fixture data (parent/2, likes/2) chosen to exercise quoting and variable rendering. Contract-level by construction: the file exists to pin the snapshot FORMAT, which is part of the published ABI.

The measured benchmark world (6 .pl files, 1,630 clauses), GENERATED IN THE OPEN by bench/world/generate.mjs — a fixed LCG, no clock, and its whole vocabulary (24 given names, 10 surnames, 10 roles, 8 factions, 10 quest titles) is literal in the generator, which is committed beside it. Nothing here was copied from a closed pack; `node bench/world/generate.mjs --check` reproduces the committed bytes from the committed source, which is the strongest form this argument can take. It is a fixture for docs/SWIPL_MEASUREMENT.md, not authoring content.

Same directory, seen by the native-specific world/pack path rule: the generator, MANIFEST.json (sha256 per file), QUERIES.txt and README.md alongside the six .pl files. Classified once, for the reason above. This is the rule doing its job — a directory literally named `world/` in the engine repository is exactly what a human should be made to look at before the flip; the answer here is that it is a reproducible benchmark fixture.
